results.question: Are body measurements like waist size linked to height?
claims: In NHANES III adults, waist circumference scaled to height after adjustment for age and race, with powers of 0.76 in men and 0.80 in women (both P<0.001), corresponding to roughly 0.2 to 0.5 cm increase in circumference per cm of height.
Waist circumference/height and hip circumference/height ratios scaled negatively to height in both sexes, so these ratios are not height-independent. WC/HC scaled negatively to height in women only.

Other studies also link height with waist size: in Glasgow, residents of the most deprived neighbourhood were shorter and had larger waist circumferences, and in Manchester lower height and greater waist girth were independently related to plasma glucose.

results.question: Can the brain's right half learn to read on its own?
claims: In seven individuals who had left cerebral hemispherectomy, so reading depended on the right hemisphere, about 60% developed average-range word and paragraph reading.

Phonological processing, measured by phonological awareness and nonword reading, was unexpectedly spared in most of these participants, and phonological awareness correlated strongly with word reading.
Verbal memory and receptive vocabulary correlated positively with reading levels, similar to relationships reported in average readers, and later seizure onset was associated with better reading.

results.question: Does keyhole surgery hurt newborns less than open surgery?
claims: In a retrospective matched cohort of neonates having thoracoscopic minimal access surgery versus conventional surgery for esophageal atresia or congenital diaphragmatic hernia, cumulative opioid doses did not differ significantly at 12 h, 24 h, 48 h or 7 days.
Postoperative pain scores were also similar between the minimal access and conventional groups, so this study found no evidence that keyhole surgery reduced pain in newborns.

results.question: Does a stroke patient's sex change how well the clot-busting drug rt-PA works?
claims: In a multicenter series of 369 rt-PA-treated stroke patients monitored with transcranial Doppler, men and women did not differ in complete, partial or no recanalization, time to recanalization, or 3-month outcome, including after adjustment for covariates.

In a large register of 45,079 alteplase-treated patients, women had worse unadjusted functional independence and mortality, but after adjustment there was no sex difference in functional outcome (OR 1.03, 95% CI 0.97-1.09).

results.question: Is trouble putting feelings into words linked to unexplained physical symptoms?
claims: Evidence is mixed: in an internal medicine outpatient clinic, patients with medically unexplained symptoms were overall not more alexithymic than those with explained symptoms, and alexithymia was not linked to subjective health experience or use of medical services.
A subgroup of patients with unexplained symptoms and a mental disorder who denied any connection between emotional problems and physical symptoms did show more alexithymic traits.

results.question: Can third-trimester ultrasound predict the position of the first twin at delivery?
claims: Noncephalic presentation of twin A on sonogram predicted noncephalic presentation at delivery with a positive predictive value above 90% after 32 weeks of gestation.

results.question: Are people with serious mental illness more likely to end up in worse nursing homes?
claims: In a national cohort of over 1.3 million new nursing home admissions in 2007, patients with schizophrenia or bipolar disorder tended to enter nursing homes with more total and healthcare-related deficiency citations than other patients.

Patients with schizophrenia entered facilities with more total (13.3 vs. 11.2) and healthcare-related deficiencies (8.6 vs. 7.2), and patients with bipolar disorder likewise entered facilities with more total (12.5 vs. 11.2) and healthcare-related deficiencies (8.2 vs. 7.2).

The association of serious mental illness with admission to higher-deficiency nursing homes persisted after controlling for within-county facility choice, patient characteristics, and facility covariates.

results.question: Do recorded lectures make medical students skip class?
claims: In a survey study of first-year graduate-entry medical students given prerecorded Physiology VODcasts, 84.3% attended all 21 live lectures and only 4% missed more than one lecture per series, so recorded lectures did not appear to cause widespread skipping.
79% of these students indicated that VODcasts should not replace live lectures.

results.question: Is paying pregnant smokers to quit worth the cost?
claims: A cost-effectiveness analysis of a Glasgow RCT of up to £400 in vouchers for pregnant smokers found an incremental cost of £1127 per cotinine-validated quitter at 34-38 weeks of pregnancy, and a lifetime model gave an ICER of £482/QALY, well below a £30,000/QALY willingness-to-pay threshold.
The cost per quitter was similar to the £1390 per quitter obtained from published ICER look-up tables, based on an incremental cost of £157 and an incremental 6-month quit outcome of 0.14.
The lifetime model showed a small incremental cost (£17) and a small QALY gain (0.04).

results.question: Does a baby's sex affect asthma ER visits during pregnancy?
claims: Fetal gender was not associated with the risk of an ED visit for asthma during pregnancy (OR 1.01, 95% CI 0.85-1.19) in a linked database study of 109,173 live singleton deliveries, 530 of which involved an asthma ED visit.
Among women who had an asthma ED visit during pregnancy, fetal gender also did not significantly predict adverse pregnancy outcomes (low birth weight, preterm delivery, Caesarian delivery).

results.question: Can adults with mild intellectual disabilities get better at reading comprehension?
claims: In a study of 38 adults with mild intellectual disability, a 15-week text comprehension strategy program (summarizing, questioning, clarifying, predicting) produced substantial transfer gains in general text comprehension.
The gains in general reading comprehension were well maintained at follow-up, and direct effects on the trained strategy tests were substantial except for the questioning strategy.
Individual instruction and small-group reciprocal teaching did not differ significantly in effectiveness.

results.question: Is breast cancer prognosis inherited?
claims: In a Swedish population-based cohort, daughters and sisters of a breast cancer patient with poor prognosis had a 60% higher 5-year breast cancer mortality than relatives of a patient with good prognosis (HR 1.6; 95% CI 1.2-2.2), suggesting prognosis is familial.
Five-year survival was lower among daughters whose mothers died within 5 years (87% vs 91%) and among sisters whose proband sister died within 5 years (70% vs 88%).
The association was slightly stronger among sisters (HR 1.8; 95% CI 1.0-3.4) than among daughters (HR 1.6; 95% CI 1.1-2.3).

results.question: Are rural Australian patients willing to help teach medical students?
claims: In a survey of patients at rural and regional New South Wales general practices, 118 of 122 patients consented to medical student involvement in their consultation, and patients were overwhelmingly positive about their practice being involved in student teaching.
Patients felt they played an important role in teaching, and after the consultation they reported they would have accepted higher levels of student involvement than actually occurred.
Before consultations, patients were reluctant to let students conduct some or all aspects of the consultation independently.
